questions.q: How does a content-based recommender build a user profile in this lesson?
options: By averaging the ratings of the user's friends
By counting the user's total number of clicks
By clustering users into two taste groups
By summing the TF-IDF vectors of the items the user clicked
questions.explain: Multiplying the click matrix by the item TF-IDF matrix adds up the vectors of every item a user clicked, giving a profile in word space.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of content-based recommendation over collaborative filtering?
options: It never needs any item data
It can score a brand-new item using only its description, before anyone has clicked it
It always gives more accurate results
It removes the need for user profiles
questions.explain: A new item only needs a description to be vectorized and compared with user profiles, so it avoids the item cold-start problem.

questions.q: In the lesson, a camping chair appeared among the items most similar to an office chair. What does this illustrate?
options: Cosine similarity is broken
Camping chairs are popular with office workers
Matching on words can link items that share vocabulary but not purpose
TF-IDF always ignores nouns
questions.explain: The two descriptions share words like chair, so word-based similarity connects them. Content-based methods are only as good as the item text.

questions.q: What is the filter-bubble limitation of content-based recommenders?
options: They can only recommend items the user has already clicked
They tend to recommend more of what the user already liked, with few surprises
They require every user to rate every item
They cannot explain their recommendations
questions.explain: Because scores come from similarity to past clicks, recommendations stay close to existing tastes. Hybrids and exploration help break out.

questions.q: Why do production systems often use hybrid recommenders?
options: To combine content-based scores for new items with collaborative scores where history exists
Because a hybrid is always cheaper to run
Because collaborative filtering cannot use cosine similarity
Because content-based methods only work on numeric data
questions.explain: Each family has complementary strengths and weaknesses; blending content-based and collaborative signals covers cold start and history-rich cases.
